title: Heterogeneous GPU headroom miscount causing silent dedicated shortfalls
creator: Priya Natarajan
description: Multiple enterprise customers observed silent capacity shortfalls in Reserved Pools which manifested as increased cold-starts and higher p95 latency during burst traffic windows. Initial triage showed autoscaler did not add headroom quickly enough for tenants using GPU variants with lower vCPU equivalence, causing the scheduler to under-allocate across heterogeneous pools. This ticket tracks the investigation, immediate mitigations, hotfix rollout, and follow-up reliability work.
timeline: 2026-03-09 09:12 - Pager alert: Reserved-pool-az-3 utilization hit 98% for reserved-pool-id rp-84; spike in tenant error rate reported by monitoring (acme-health)
2026-03-09 09:25 - Customer support escalated to SRE and PM; initial mitigation: increase tenant burst fallback timeout to 30s

2026-03-10 14:00 - Deeper investigation started by autoscaler team; repro tests run against sim cluster with heterogeneous GPU types
2026-03-11 16:30 - Identified headroom calc uses normalized vCPU heuristics that assume homogeneous GPU-vCPU mapping; miscount occurs when heterogenous GPU types mixed in same AZ
2026-03-12 08:20 - Hotfix branch created to include GPU-type weight adjustment and per-GPU-type headroom accounting (PR: github.com/redwood-inference/autoscaler/pull/1297)

investigation_notes: Root analysis combined telemetry from reserved-pool allocator, lease table, and VM/GPU capacity exporter. Two compounding failures found: (1) headroom estimator normalized all GPU SKUs to a single vCPU-equivalent value derived from an outdated SKU map, causing underestimation for older high-memory GPUs; (2) burst-credit reconciler omitted pending preemptible vCPU reservations during a scale-up window, so autoscaler believed more free capacity was available than actually committed. Additionally, KV cache pressure caused eviction spikes which increased request latencies in a feedback loop.
root_cause: Autoscaler headroom estimator used a stale GPU-to-vCPU normalization map and lacked per-GPU-type accounting. This led to underprovisioning when heterogeneous GPU SKUs were present. The burst-credit reconciler race allowed temporary double-counting of available headroom. Together these caused reserved pools to appear healthier than they were and delayed scale-ups until backpressure had already impacted customers.
mitigation: Immediate: enable safe fallback policy that routes high-priority tenants to dedicated cold fallback pools and increases burst timeout for enterprise plans
Hotfix: update headroom estimator to use live SKU weights and per-GPU-type buckets (PR: github.com/redwood-inference/autoscaler/pull/1297)
Hotfix: add short-circuit in scale controller to trigger emergency scale-ups when p95 latency or queue depth thresholds breached despite headroom > 0
Telemetry: instrument lease-table commit traces and add alerts for discrepancy between reported and committed capacity
Customer comms: notify impacted customers with timeline and mitigation steps; offer credits if SLA breach confirmed

postmortem_summary: Contributing factors included stale SKU normalization, burst-credit reconciler race, and insufficient telemetry around committed vs available capacity. The hotfix (autoscale-2.4.0-hotfix) restores per-GPU-type accounting, adds emergency scale triggers, and improves telemetry. Canary results are positive; we will monitor for three full traffic cycles before closing the incident and will schedule a follow-up to harden unit tests and add cross-region chaos tests.
comms: Prepared customer-facing post explaining root cause and mitigations. Sent initial notification to impacted accounts on 2026-03-13 and follow-up on 2026-03-14 with expected timeline for full rollout. Internal all-hands summary posted to #incidents channel.
